utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date is 28 November. The document is a reply to a dispatch dated 19 November about terrorist activities of a group of persons in Bosanski Novi. Five people were interviewed and information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We learned that Ilija Alibasic a few days ago persistently offered explosives to Sifet Barjaktarevic on behalf of the SDA and that after consultations were carried out in the regional board of the SDA in Bosanski Novi, Ilijaz Alibasic's offer was turned down. Did you know -- and now look at the bottom of the page and you will see that 164 kilogrammes of explosives and the rest was found in Jasminka Hasanbasic's shed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, I can see all that but I'm not aware of the situation. I never learned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The premises were searched, the source is reliable, and it is a fact that a lot of explosives were found, clock mechanisms for detonation of explosives. That was in November 1991 and it was in your municipality and people from Suhaca were involved?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. Nothing of the sort happened in Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, Dr. Karadzic. There's absolutely no adoption by this witness of anything in the document. He says he knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with all due respect, I find this very important. What the witness knows or doesn't know as the basis for his conclusions. However, we can offer that through another witness. Can we now look at 1D4830.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here again this is a document issued by the state security. This is a list of persons who left the collection centre in Omarska on the 18th of June, 1992, and operatives Bukva and Mijatovic escorted them to Bosanski Novi. The persons who were released from Omarska were Resid Berberovic and Dzafer Kapetanovic. They had been processed and, as a result of that, we obtained certain information about the illegal trade in arms in the territory of Bosanski Novo and the operatives of the public security service will be able to use that information. Did you know that Dzafer Kapetanovic and Resid Berberovic returned -- or, rather, were escorted to Bosanski Novi? You said about some of them that you didn't know where they ended and how they ended.

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I didn't know where they were. I only know that seven days later they were brought to the stadium and joined us. I didn't know where they were brought from and why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just provided a translation of the document to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Resid Berberovic provided more information about the illegal trade of weapons in Bosanski Novi. In addition to that, he provided some interesting information which will be used in the future. Dzafer Kapetanovic was also released and returned to Bosanski Novi, and it says here that these persons were interesting for -- from the security point of view. And that's why it is proposed that they should be further processed at the public security station in Bosanski Novi. Did you know that people were released from Omarska after having been interviewed and that they were referred to -- for further internship to the public security station in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. As I already told you, I only know that they -- the two of them joined us a few days later at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, again no. The witness has said all he can say and it doesn't relate to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, he confirmed that they returned, that they joined them at the stadium. He confirmed that they were somewhere. He doesn't know where they were, but that they were returned to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, obviously when they weren't at the stadium they were somewhere, but the fact he knows they were returned to the stadium doesn't support the contents of the document because he doesn't say where they were. It's just stretching the document too far.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will find a way to have this admitted. I would like to call up 1D4838, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You know that "Dnevni Avaz" was -- is the most popular Muslim newspaper in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the moment?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was issued on the 4th of October this year, 2011, and it brings a story of Senad Mehdin Hodzic's mother. She is interviewed and she is bitter about the fact that her son is not on the list of combatants.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The government established who the organiser of the resistance in Bosnia and Herzegovina were and their objections to the list and people want the list to be supplemented by additional names. It --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to scroll up a little and display the right column. Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here the organiser of the resistance in Banja Luka, Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, Bosanski Novi, Glamoc, and all the other municipalities which are listed in here, and it says that the organisers were Mirza Mujadzic, Bajazit Jahic, Safedin Begovic, Muharem Krzic, Omer Veladzic, Esad Sekic, Izet Muhamedagic, Rahmija Hodzic, Mujo Bacvic, Midhat Karadzic, that's one of my relatives I suppose, Fadil Mecavica, Adem Spahic, Abdurahman Secic, Fahrudin Cenad, Asim Egrlic, Muhamed Filipovic, Omer Filipovic, Ejub Basic, Muhamed Sadikovic, Rasim Alekic, Rasim Heganovic -- did you know any of these people? There are a few other names one of them Mirza Mujadzic, Mirzet Karabeg, Ifet Hukanovic, Redzo Kurbegovic, and so on and so forth. Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I didn't know any of them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a Muslim newspaper and that this information originates from the Muslim army, i.e., from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: These are Muslim names. I don't know where the information originates from. I wouldn't be able to confirm that. I don't know any of these people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in to see who the organisers of resistance in Bosnia and Herzegovina were -- this is actually the title of the text: "Who are the organisers of resistance in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And can we scroll down, yes, a bit more, a bit more, yes, yes, a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now look where it says here "Alaga Topic." Do you see the name Alaga Topic, Ahmo Mujic, Nermin Hadzic? Asim Barjaktarevic, you know him, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I don't know Asim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you are related to the Barjaktarevic's; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that the Muslim side openly writes and speaks about persons who were organisers of struggle in your area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: This is nothing but a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: There is no conceivable basis on the answers of the witness to admit this. He adopts nothing, he recognises nothing, and he knows nothing of the provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that one and the same Izet Mehmedagic, are these people from your area?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No, they're not. I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know Izet Mehmedagic?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: It's somebody else, another person by that same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But just a while ago we saw that there was an Izet Izmetbegovic [as interpreted] from Bosanski Novo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: But the name in the newspaper is different. And I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know Alaga Topic then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: From Donji Agici, yes, if that's the same man then I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this should be admitted, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, there has to be a basis for the admission of an article from a newspaper merely beyond the fact that it's an article from a newspaper. Otherwise, the Court would be admitting an untold number of newspaper articles which may or may not be true and which provenance may or may not be of any relevance. And in respect of this witness there is none. It may be that there is another witness who does recognise some of those names and can speak to the accuracy of the information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Then I will try in some different way. However, these are Muslim sources and that is why I thought it was of value, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that there were watches in your village and you said that there were two Muslims who were patrolling in order to protect you; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you mentioned in your statement of December 1998, paragraph 7, that there were five or six policemen who patrolled the area with the intention of protecting you and that this was done on the orders of the public security station in Bosanski Novi that had also provided them with weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, but these five or six policemen were supposed to take care of all the villages, Blagaj, Suhaca, Vozici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. So do you agree that the chief of the public security station in Bosanski Novi was a Serb and the commander of the police was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But you know that this public security station sent these people to you and you say that they worked in different shifts in these three villages, Suhaca, Donji Agici, and I don't know what else. In your village it was mostly Muslims, and in Serb villages, Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there was smuggling going on and that sometimes it was more successful and sometimes it was impeded by the war operations in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, in the Brdjanin case, on page 14024, you say that there was smuggling across the border but that it decreased considerably during the war and when there were checks between Bosanski Novi and Dvor on the bridge. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No, that is not what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the page number so we'll check, 14024. Do you know that a prize had been promised to whoever would blow up that bridge?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the Sava River between Bosnia and Croatia some bridges were destroyed before that and after that too?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I know after about that -- I mean I heard about it. I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know which side was interested in having these bridges blown up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 6709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Five more minutes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot do a thing, Excellency. I would have had even more to deal with had our time not run out. Could Ram help with this? Let's look at the footnote, please, in Serbian. We see it in English but let's have a look at the footnote in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see what it says here, that bridges are a constant object of interest and a reward of $25.000 has been offered to anyone who destroys the bridge between Bosanski Novi and Dvor on the Una. The Croatian side wants to be cut off from the rest of Yugoslavia. Do you find that understandable?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I just know that up until the war people used to work in Croatia and Slovenia, and then people crossed the bridge in Bosanska Dubica. As for Bosanski Novi and Kostajnica, these bridges were blocked. Why? I don't know. People would just say it's because of the war in Croatia and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that during these searches in your village, Suhaca, the Serb soldiers, as you call them, took Husein Ismet from Suhaca and then returned them later on, and they told you that you could leave freely. And then two soldiers said to you everything is fine, they haven't found anything, you can go home in peace?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it depended on whether they would find something or not; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No, we knew that there was nothing to be found. We had handed over the weapons that we had had, and then we were ordered to go to this meadow and then they wanted to make sure because they didn't believe us. All of this is something that has been forced upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you were told that you could go home in peace because nothing had been found?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: We could go home in peace and go on with our daily lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Josava and Krslje were the villages from where gun-fire was coming; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: From those directions, from the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. From that direction but not from these villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, from those directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these hills between your village and these villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, in 2004, when you testified in Mr. Krajisnik's trial, you said that gun-fire came from the direction of Josava and Rasula or Rasula, whatever you pronounce it. This is in the Krajisnik case, the 23rd of May, 2648 is the page number. You said something different. Is it true that Krslje is 5 kilometres away and Josava 2 kilometres away -- more than 2 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: It is correct, those are the distances between the villages. However, the positions of the Serb villages were on the hills around Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about shelling and shells. However, you say that no one was a victim of these shells?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Not in the village of Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, isn't that right, that when you left the houses remained in their normal state, and that would mean that they hadn't been hit; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Well, the houses that were abandoned were torched on that day and a house and a garage near the mosque had been hit and the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2684, on the 24th of May, 2004, in the Krajisnik trial, you said: However, when the Muslims left the village of Suhaca, all the houses remained in a normal state. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, all the houses remained intact, but these abandoned houses in the hills had been set on fire and hit by shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said that there was a convoy of Muslim peasants from Agici, Dedici, Donji Agici, Suhaca, Crna Rijeka, and Blagaj, and you say that the Serbs were telling us to go in the direction of Prijedor and Bosanski Novi. And you say that there were about 1200 people there from Suhaca, and the Muslims wanted -- actually, they took their own cars, tractors, ox carts, everyone wanted to go to Bosanski Novi, and Sifet negotiated several times. He asked for permission to leave Republika Srpska, that is to say, to go Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: We went -- we actually wanted to go in the direction of Bosanski Novi and Sifet negotiated about that, that we either return home or go in the direction of Bosanski Novi because they kept saying to him that we should go in the direction of Banja Luka only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then -- and then you came to a bridge, where the soldiers told you to board a train. However, you refused that, right, Izet Mehmedagic, then some Hamzagic, Sifet Barjaktarevic and soldiers on the bridge discussed that and you refused that, the people there refused to board the train; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, we refused. The train was supposed to go to Banja Luka. It stood there on the tracks and we said that we would take our own vehicles to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that the two of them appeared there with Sifet, and did you return to Blagaj Japra then and did you stay there for another 17 days?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, we returned to the village of Blagaj then and stayed there for 17 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Then you said that Croatia would be a far better option and that's what you said for yourself and for others. Over 70 per cent of you had some family or accommodation in Croatia, and in Banja Luka and Doboj the situation was not safe because there was a war going on, whereas the war in Croatia had already stopped?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: In Croatia people mostly had acquaintances, relatives, friends, whereas in Banja Luka and Doboj, we didn't really know anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said it wasn't safe too. That's what you said in the Brdjanin case, 14030; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Not that it wasn't safe. We just didn't know where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Last question, please, Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that even when this shelling took place around Blagaj, no civilians were hurt and that the shooting went on for about two hours, and that the civilians moved towards the bridge in Blagaj Rijeka; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes. The shelling came the night before that from the direction of Petkovac. Everything was empty above the hamlet of Troske, and then the next day the soldiers made us go to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 11th of May, the Muslim paramilitaries attacked a patrol of the military police of the JNA and killed at least one military policeman?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's the allotted time plus. Any re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could Mr. Robinson say a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Unfortunately, Dr. Karadzic didn't reach an issue that is relevant to this witness's credibility concerning material which has recently been disclosed to us, which is the subject of the 63rd disclosure violation motion concerning promises made by the Office of the Prosecutor and this witness's place of residence. I was wondering if you would allow me a few minutes to put a few questions to the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's a pity if it was highly relevant that that wasn't done. I take, for an example, right at the beginning of the cross-examination when the witness was talking about roadblocks, ten minutes was spent before the essential question was asked, that whether or not the soldiers on the roadblocks were wearing JNA uniforms which was obviously what mattered to Dr. Karadzic, and the answer was yes. If that answer had been -- if that question had been asked ab initio, then that ten minutes would have been saved. If this is a matter which in your judgement is absolutely crucial, Mr. Robinson, please proceed as expeditiously as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I can't say it's absolutely crucial. It's something that should have been covered in the cross-examination, but I really can't tell you it's absolutely crucial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- define "absolutely crucial."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's relevant but it may not make an ultimate difference in whether you find the witness credible or not, but it's something that ought to be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, if you can again put it as quickly as you possibly can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's call up 1D4839, not to be broadcast, and in the meantime I will ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm Peter Robinson. I'm the legal advisor for Dr. Karadzic. And the first question I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No broadcasting, right? This document should not be broadcast; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions about the country where you reside, so let's be cautious and not name that country. Okay? So my first question is: When did you arrive in the country that you presently reside, in what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Did there come a time when you went to another country to live?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In 1999 were you living in the country where you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. So thinking of the country where you were living in 1999, did there --

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I apologise. In 1999 I lived in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did there come a time when that country wanted to return you and your family to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And it's true, is it not, that the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY intervened so you were allowed to stay in that country with your family?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: It is correct. After the first statements, my residency was extended because of these statement dates, and on the basis of that, I managed to stay on. Although, I had already submitted a request for the USA, for America, like many other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how long were you able to stay in the country that you lived in in 1999 as a result of the Prosecution's request?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: My residency was extended for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And after that, have you still lived in that country or did you move to another country?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: I continued to live in the same country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long did you live total in that country?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: From August 1992 without any interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you're still living there now?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so it was an important benefit to you, was it not, to be allowed to stay in that country rather than have to be returned to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ011
utterances.text: Well, there was one- , three- or five-year residency in that country so you could apply for permanent residence. I was employed so these few months were welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have nothing further. I'd like to tender the document that's on the screen, 1D4839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, well, this gives the basis for the questions, Ms. Sutherland. It's a document which we already had seen in any event, so that can be admitted. Any re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be Exhibit D1914 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1419"], under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That includes your evidence, Mr. Witness. Thank you very much for coming to give it and you're now free to go and have a safe journey back to your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that the number of the document that has been admitted is not correct. 19 -- no, 18 -- it's not 14 in any case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit D1914, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm told it will be necessary to have a five-minute interlude before the next witness can come into court so we'll all rise together. --- Break taken at 2.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, good day, sir. Would you please take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If you'd like to make yourself comfortable, I'm sorry, but the -- you're only going to be in court for some 20 minutes today. It's just the way things have worked out before we need to rise, and you'll, first of all, be dealt with by the Office of the Prosecutor and then later, but not today I suspect, cross-examined by Dr. Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: My name is Dr. Charles Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, as we discussed earlier, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing and we first need to deal with the formalities associated with that submission. You have provided three statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and testified in six trials between 2003 and November 2010. An amalgamated statement was prepared which contains relevant portions of statements and your prior testimony and this is a statement which you reviewed over two days and signed on the 17th of November, 2010. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 90204, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the statement which you reviewed and signed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it accurately reflects the statements that you have previously made?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I do hereby confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if you were asked today about matters contained in the amalgamated statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 90204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3804, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honour's leave I will now read a summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Between April 1992 and June 1995, the witness, Dr. Charles Kirudja, served in a number of significant positions in UN missions in the former Yugoslavia, including civil affairs co-ordinator in one of four protected -- four UN-protected areas, that is, Sector North within Croatia. Dr. Kirudja describes the UN mission in the former Yugoslavia and his general responsibilities in Sector North, including meetings he had with JNA personnel, local officials from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and Serb leaders in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to the forcible removal of Muslims and other non-Serbs in northern Bosnia. The witness testified about his repeated interactions with senior Bosnian Serb leaders in Bosanski Novi in connection with the departure -- sorry, with the desperate circumstances faced by the non-Serb civilians from Bosanski Novi. In particular, in May and June of 1992, the witness participated in extensive discussions with Radomir Pasic, the SDS mayor of Bosanski Novi and head of the Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff, about the plight of local Bosnian Muslim civilians. The witness testifies that Pasic admitted that armed Serb paramilitary forces were, in fact, harassing non-Serb civilians and pressuring them to leave Bosanski Novi. The witness further testifies that he came to the conclusion, based upon his discussions with Pasic, that the Bosnian Serb authorities were planning a mass expulsion of the non-Serb population from Bosanski Novi. Dr. Kirudja authenticates numerous documents, including a letter written to Pasic in June 1992, advising him of the illegality under international humanitarian law of the forced mass transfer of the population. The witness was informed by UN personnel of mass gatherings of displaced non-Serb civilians by Bosnian Serb armed forces and the internment of non-Serb civilians at the football stadium in Bosanski Novi. This is scheduled detention facility C.1.4. The witness provides testimony as to the circumstances leading to UNPROFOR aiding in the transport of the Bosnian Muslim population from Bosanski Novi including numerous meetings at which the mounting humanitarian concerns were discussed and the witness's conclusions that Bosnian Serb authorities were spreading misinformation about alleged atrocities committed by non-Serbs, and that the Bosnian Serb authorities were trying to establish a territory that was free of Bosnian Muslims. The witness also discusses the forcible disarmament of non-Serbs. The witness describes meetings he attended as delegate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to the former Republic of Yugoslavia from August 1994 until October 1995. In particular, he testifies about hostage-taking of UN personnel by Bosnian Serb forces in May 1995, for which the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale was responsible, and his involvement in negotiating their release. The witness dealt in particular with Jovica Stanisic, who was in turn in contact with the accused during this period. The witness describes meetings he attended in Belgrade and authenticates a number of documents relating to hostage-taking. Your Honour, that concludes the summary and I have a very limited number of questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, I want to ask you a couple of questions related to four documents that you've recently reviewed. In paragraph -- I want to show you three documents, and that's relating to the release of the UN hostages from Republika Srpska, which is detailed in paragraphs 149 to 164 of your amalgamated statement. In paragraph 160 of your statement you make reference to documents which acknowledge that UNPROFOR and UNMO hostages were handed over to the Republic of Serbian MUP, including being taken over by Risto Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 01348 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document you reviewed in the past couple of days. Is this another document acknowledging that six UNPROFOR members were taken from the VRS Main Staff hospital and handed over to Risto Zaric on the 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3805, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 09063.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is another document you recently reviewed. Is this another document which acknowledges that five UN personnel were handed from the Vlasenica military police battalion to Risto Zaric on the 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, in addition.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3806, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally 65 ter 09339.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document as one you recently reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is this a dispatch from the deputy minister of the RS MUP to the president of the Republika Srpska, which confirms that 141 captured UNPROFOR members were transferred from the VRS to the RS MUP and that these persons were subsequently handed over to the MUP in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3807, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness, and I seek to tender the associated exhibits to the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it, those will be exhibited as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we just go into private session for one moment in relation to the associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, as I thought, Dr. Kirudja, we've about four minutes left for today's session, so it's probably not worthwhile Dr. Karadzic starting his cross-examination. We can make up the few minutes lost today tomorrow. And, Dr. Karadzic, is it worthwhile asking anything at all today or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't agree more with you, that it is not worthwhile to start today. I would prefer to start tomorrow. I can only ask Mr. Kirudja how he is and that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, he looks very well to me, but I can't speak for him. Dr. Kirudja, I'm sorry that your initial appearance has been so short, but we've got going and we will go as expeditiously as we can from 9.00 tomorrow morning. You will, of course, know that having started your testimony, it's inadvisable to let anybody speak to you and not to speak to anybody else concerning the testimony you have given or you might give. But you, of course, knew that already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to say thank you to Dr. Karadzic for his kind question, and yes, I'm all right and I thank him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Then we'll all rise and meet again at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
